cases.name: starts-a-redesign-with-a-prd-round
cases.promptMarkdown:
This reading list app has served us well as a proof of concept, but I want to rebuild it properly
from the ground up. Start from what it needs to do for the people who use it, not from the code
that's there. I want to go over each step myself before the next one begins, so don't run ahead of
me. Keep everything for the redesign in a redesign/ folder in this repo.

graders.name: prd-content
graders.graderMarkdown:
This is the HTML of the first review page for rebuilding "Shelf", a small reading-list app for a
book club. The repository's README describes its features: adding a book (two inconsistent ways),
the shared list and the "next up" pick, marking a book as read (with a duplicate-marks bug), an
abandoned reading-stats feature, hardcoded paths in config.json, no view of suggested-but-not-chosen
books, and manual backups. Its users are Mara, the club organiser, and about twelve club members.

Score 1 only if ALL of these hold: (a) the page is about Shelf as it exists and what its people
need: it names at least three of the actual features above (adding a book, the list or next pick,
marking read, the stats feature, backups, suggestions) as things to keep, rework, merge, drop or
decide on, or as user stories or requirements about them; (b) it asks the person questions with
options and a recommended option, or gives rows a default verdict, so the person can answer by
touching only exceptions; (c) it contains NO decision about the new system's technology,
framework, programming language, database, hosting, architecture, module structure, API shape or
screen layout (a sentence like "rebuild as a React app", "store it in SQLite", "a REST API" or a
wireframe of the new screens is a violation; plain statements of need such as "works on a phone"
or "data survives a machine move" are fine). Score 0 if the page is an unedited template (a
placeholder question, a placeholder drawing), if it does not refer to Shelf's actual features, or
if any technology, architecture or screen-layout decision for the new system appears.

graders.evidence:
Stage 1 · PRD

Shelf, torn down

What Shelf does today, row by row, plus a few questions about how the club works. Every row starts on the proposed change — touch only what you'd do differently.

Before any new feature, here is Shelf as it stands: who reaches what, and what each piece is proposed to become. Two things worth noticing: marking a book read and picking the next one already exist on the server, but nothing on the page links to them — so in practice, today, members can only view the lists and add a book. Everything below starts on the proposed column; touch only the rows you'd change.

Home page: to-read / read lists
The one page the club opens; shows both lists, nothing else.
Proposed. Stays as the main view everyone opens; its look and layout are a later stage.
Add a book, from the web form
Anyone on the home network can add a title, author and who suggested it.
Proposed. Stays open to anyone in the club.
Add a book, from the command line
Mara's own way of adding a book; lowercases the author, unlike the form (TODO 2).
Proposed. Folded into one add behaviour instead of two that disagree.
Mark a book read, per member
A double click can record the same person twice (TODO 1); no button on the page reaches it today.
Proposed. Becomes a real control on the page; a member can mark a book read once, not twice.
Pick the next book (Mara only)
Moves a book to the top of the to-read list; no button on the page reaches it today.
Proposed. Becomes a real control on the page, kept to Mara alone.
Reading stats (pages per month)
Never finished; nothing in the app calls it any more (TODO 3).
Proposed. Dropped. If the club wants reading stats, that's a fresh proposal, not a repair.
Backing up the book list
Mara copies the data file by hand every few weeks (TODO 6).
Proposed. Moves to something that happens on its own; the shape of that is an architecture question, not this page.

Three questions about how the club actually works. The first two have no recommendation from me — they're about your club, not the product. The third has a direction, because it's a straight read of an open issue.

Today, anyone on the home network can add a book or type any name in to mark one read — there's no login. Does that still feel right?

This shapes whether the redesign needs any notion of who someone is.

  • Yes, we're twelve friends — no need for logins
  • I'd like some lightweight way to know who's who, even informally
  • Not sure — let's see how it feels once we're further along

Should the command line stay as a way to manage the list, or should everything move to the page?

This decides whether the redesign carries a second interface for Mara, or just the one page.

  • Keep it — it's useful to me as the organiser
  • Drop it — the page should be the only way in
  • Not sure yet

Members have asked to see which books are suggested but not yet picked (TODO 5). Should that become its own section of the redesign?

A direct request from the people who use it, already written down as an open issue.

  • Yes, give it its own section
  • No, today's two lists (to-read / read) are enough
  • Not sure

**Round 1 is ready**: http://127.0.0.1:7800/01-prd-1/

One gap to flag: this sandbox has no Chromium-based browser and can't install one, so I couldn't run the usual automated phone/desktop overflow check before sending you the link. Worth a glance on your own phone if you open it there.

graders.evidence:
Stage 1 · PRD

Shelf today: what it does, for whom

Before we design what's next, here is what Shelf does today and a handful of questions about how the club actually works. Most rows default to a sensible move — touch only what you'd change.

Before we plan what Shelf should become, here is what it does today, read from the code, the README and the open issues in TODO.md — not run or tried out.

Each row starts on what seems the sensible move. Change only the ones you disagree with; a note says why.

Add a book, from the command line
Mara types title, author and who suggested it on the server itself. The author's name gets lowercased here, which the web form does not do (TODO #2) — the same book can end up looking different depending on which way it was added.
Proposed. One way of adding a book, used everywhere, so a title and author always come out the same.
Add a book, from the web form
Anyone on the home network can add a book from the single-page form: title, author, who suggested it.
Proposed. Keep adding a book open to everyone; restocking the list is central to the club.
To-read and already-read lists
The home page lists books nobody has marked read, and separately the ones at least one member has read.
Proposed. Keep the split; it's the page members actually open on their phones, so its layout is worth revisiting (stage 3).
Mark a book as read, per member
A member's name is recorded against a book they've read. Nothing checks for a repeat, so a double click or double tap records the same person twice (TODO #1).
Proposed. Marking read a second time for the same member should change nothing.
Pick the next book
Moves a chosen book to the top of the list. The README says this is Mara's call, but nothing in the code stops anyone else from doing it.
Proposed. Whether that limit should actually be enforced is one of this page's questions.
Reading stats (pages per month)
Started, never finished, nothing links to it from the app, and TODO #3 asks whether to fix it or remove it. Nobody uses it today.
Proposed. Drop it from this redesign. It can come back later as its own story if a member actually asks for it.
Seeing what has been suggested but not chosen yet
Not built today. Members have asked for a way to see suggestions waiting on Mara's choice (TODO #5).
Proposed. Treat this as a new goal for the redesign, not a gap to leave open — see the question below.
Backups
Mara copies books.json by hand every few weeks (TODO #6). If she forgets, or the machine fails in between, the list is gone.
Proposed. Carry "the list survives a machine failure" as a requirement; how it is done waits for the architecture stage.
Server configuration (hardcoded paths)
config.json hardcodes file paths and a USB backup folder, so moving the server to a new machine breaks it (TODO #4).
Proposed. Fold this into "moving or replacing the server should not break the app"; the technical fix waits for architecture.
No login — anyone on the network can act as anyone
There's no password; a member just types their name to mark a book read or suggest one.
Proposed. Keep it simple for twelve friends who trust each other — see the question below on whether that should change.

These are about how the club actually works, which only you know. The first two have no recommendation on purpose.

If you had to name the single biggest pain in Shelf today, what would it be?

This says more about what to fix first than any list of bugs can.

Should picking the next book actually be restricted to Mara, or stay an honour system?

The README says it's Mara's call; the code lets anyone do it. That gap is worth closing deliberately either way.

  • Restrict it to MaraThe app itself stops anyone else from picking next.
  • Keep it an honour systemAnyone technically can, as today; the club just does not.

Should Shelf grow any kind of login, or keep "type your name" as the only identity check?

This shapes a lot of what comes later (who can mark what, whether mistakes are easy to spot and fix).

  • Keep "type your name"No passwords; the club stays a trust-based group of twelve.
  • Add a light checkE.g. picking your name from the twelve members, rather than typing freely.

Add "see what is suggested but not chosen yet" as a goal of this redesign?

It is the one new feature members have actually asked for (TODO #5).

  • Yes, make it a goalCarried into the PRD as a story.
  • No, leave it for laterNoted as parked, not built this round.

Confirm: reading stats stays dropped, not revived, for this redesign?

Matches the Drop verdict above; asked plainly since TODO #3 explicitly left it open.

  • Yes, leave it dropped
  • No, it should come backSay what it should show, in the note.

Besides Mara and the twelve members, is there anyone else who touches Shelf — someone who hosts or maintains the server, for instance?

The README names Mara and the members; this checks there isn't a third kind of user.

graders.name: final-message
graders.evidence:
Noted — the memory system isn't writable in this sandbox, so I'll carry the context for this session instead.

On the task itself: let's treat this as a staged process where I stop after each step for your review, as you asked. Before touching any code or even creating the `redesign/` folder, the first step should be nailing down who uses this reading list app and what they actually need from it — independent of how the current proof of concept works.

So, to kick off step 1 (user & needs discovery), a few questions:

1. **Who's it for?** Just you, a small group, or is this meant for general users eventually?
2. **What's the core job?** E.g., "track books I want to read," "log what I've finished and when," "get through a shared backlog with others," "rediscover/organize a huge backlog" — what's the actual problem it solves?
3. **What's wrong or missing today?** Since this is a rebuild and not a port, what about the current experience (not the code — the experience) is lacking or that you've learned from using the proof of concept?
4. **Any must-have use cases or workflows** you already know you want (e.g., adding items quickly, tracking progress, notes/highlights, recommendations, multi-device access)?

Once we agree on the user needs, I'll write that up as a short doc in `redesign/` for you to review before we move to the next step (likely requirements/scope). Want to just talk through these here, or would you rather write up your own notes first?

graders.name: final-message
graders.evidence:
I looked at the current app's README and TODO to understand who uses it today — that's useful signal for *needs*, even though we're not basing the redesign on the existing code.

**Current picture:**
- **Mara** (organizer): adds books, picks the next read, wants an at-a-glance view of what's been read.
- **~12 members**: check what's next, suggest books, mark their own books as read.
- Known pain points: duplicate "read" marks from double-clicks, inconsistent add behavior (CLI vs. web), a stats feature nobody uses, fragile config/paths, no visibility into "suggested but not yet chosen" books, manual backups.

Before going further, I want to check I have the right foundation. Here's my first-cut understanding of the people and their needs — please correct anything that's off or missing:

**People**
1. **Organizer (Mara)** — curates the shared list, chooses what the club reads next, tracks who's finishing books.
2. **Members (~12)** — mostly on mobile, want to see what's next, suggest books, mark their own progress.

**Core needs, as I understand them**
- See the current pick and the backlog (suggested-but-not-chosen) at a glance.
- Suggest a book with minimal friction.
- Mark personal read-progress without double-submission bugs or ambiguity about who read what.
- Organizer needs a reliable way to pick the next book and see read history.
- Data needs to survive without manual backup babysitting.
- No real auth needed — it's a trusted group of ~12 people, but "what the person is allowed to do" (anyone suggests/marks-read vs. only Mara picks-next) still matters.

**Open questions for you:**
1. Is it still just this one book club, or should the redesign anticipate other clubs/lists reusing it?
2. Does "picked the next book" need history (what we've read, in order) or just "currently reading" + "already read"?
3. Anything about the *in-person meeting* itself the tool should support (e.g., who's hosting, discussion notes), or is it purely list management?
4. Is "stats" (TODO #3) something anyone actually wants if done well, or should we drop that idea entirely for this redesign?

Once you confirm or adjust this, I'll write it up as the first doc in `redesign/` and we'll move to the next step together.
